text: Everything in this chapter traces back to one 2017 paper: Vaswani and colleagues' Attention Is All You Need. This lesson closes the chapter by walking through what the paper actually proposed, in our own words and our own diagrams — never the paper's actual figures.

The title is the thesis. Before this paper, the strongest sequence models were RNN or LSTM based, processing one token at a time. This paper claims you can replace all of that recurrence with attention alone, and names the resulting architecture the Transformer.

Here's that architecture as our own diagram: embeddings plus positional encoding feed a stack of encoder layers, producing an encoder output; target embeddings plus positional encoding feed a stack of decoder layers that also look back at that encoder output, ending in a linear projection and a softmax.

Each encoder layer is self-attention plus a feed-forward sublayer. Each decoder layer is masked self-attention, then cross-attention over the encoder's output, then feed-forward. Every one of those sublayers is wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization — exactly the pattern you'll build by hand in the next chapter.

Multi-head attention gave this recurrence-free design the representational variety recurrence used to provide for free, and positional encoding gave it back the sense of order. Together, that combination turned out to scale remarkably well — which is why it's the direct ancestor of BERT, GPT, and essentially every modern large language model.
Next up, Chapter 6: building a transformer block from scratch, piece by piece, starting with the block itself.
